extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers / experimental chemists / Royal Society fellows (17th-century experimentalists)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and observational standards for conducting and reporting laboratory and field experiments in natural philosophy and chemistry (evaporation measurements, stove construction, insect rearing, flammability tests with 'spirit of nitre'). Emphasis on methods, safety, classification of materials, and interpretation of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative morphology of basalt columns
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare specimens by outward shape, columnwise formation, number and arrangement of internodia/joints, presence of a hole or pith running through joints, manner of fitting of one joint to another, sides (smooth vs sulcated/furrowed), polygonal face shape (pentagon, hexagon, heptagon), and overall size/magnitude (diameter, whether columns are entire pieces or divided into joints).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these morphological features together to judge affinity between local columns and described taxa (e.g., entrochos, astroites, lapis basaltes misenus). Note differences such as sulcated pentagonal sides versus perfectly smooth hexagonal/heptagonal faces, and whether columns are jointed or entire pieces. Consider bulk/size disparities as potentially non-fatal to affinity judgments, since nature shows disparity among allied forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaporation measurement method and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure evaporation from a known surface area over a defined time (example: surface about 8 square inches measured for a whole year), convert mass (grains) to volume (cubic inches) and compute depth evaporated per unit area (e.g., 8 inches depth per year in the experiment cited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform long-duration accumulative measurements (e.g., one year) for reliability; control for exposure to sun and wind if interested in evaporation due solely to water warmth. Compare results with other observers and regions; account for effects of wind and sun which can multiply evaporation rates; report seasonal variation (May–Aug roughly three times Nov–Feb, March/April ≈ Sept/Oct).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for vapour adhesion and optical effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that water vapours can adhere to the evaporating surface, forming a 'fleece' that reduces subsequent evaporation and has a different refractive index from common air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting evaporation and visual observations, note that a layer of vapour can cause refraction illusions (objects appear raised, ships appear above water, distant land seeming to overhang). Use still/windy comparisons to show how a persistent vapour layer reduces measured evaporation and alters visual appearance; mention as explanatory hypothesis for reported mirages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greenhouse stove installation and air distribution design
rubrics_metrics.description: For a stove to preserve plants in winter: place pipes (made of crucible earth) not too near the fire grate (about 16 inches); construct a trench the full length of the house under the paving about 18 inches wide and deep, covered with a brick arch; at trench end provide a removable square iron plate matching paving size with round holes (~3 inches) and lids to vary air release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert pipes into a channel along the wall with several openings to distribute incoming air more equally through the house; use removable coverings and adjustable holes to increase or diminish drafts and control the fire. Follow the reported dimensions as a practical design example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting severe weather event observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Record date and time, duration, magnitude (number of shocks/loads carried), distances items were transported, and credible witness accounts when reporting whirlwind/tornado events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give specific temporal markers (e.g., between one and two o'clock, continued half an hour), quantify observed effects (e.g., 80–100 shocks of corn, wagons whirled), and note reports from persons of good credit concerning long-distance carriage. Such detail strengthens the observational report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microscopic insect rearing and observation protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods for observing small insects and their life cycles: enclose specimens with food in glass tubes or boxes; prevent escape or boring by sealing corks with sealing-wax and inserting a very small glass tube to admit air; observe and record developmental milestones and timings (dates of colour changes, aurelia, moth emergence, egg counts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use small glass tubes (e.g., foot-long, finger wide) and ensure air access without allowing escape. Track individuals over time, note temperature effects (warmth of the body hastens hatching), count eggs laid (50–70 eggs example), and record days to each stage. When handling specimens, avoid overheating (pocket heat can spoil eggs); cool storage may extend development times for comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fumigation protocol for stored-grain moths
rubrics_metrics.description: To destroy prolific grain moths (larvae/moths), burn brimstone inside the storage room: in a small vessel for tests (8 moths killed in a glass by brimstone fumes), and scale up for rooms (example: for a granary 24 × 16 ft use 1/4 lb brimstone prepared as wine-coopers use, place in the middle, set on fire, shut door for two days).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat smoking as soon as moths appear and for some days successively. Sweep larvae off walls in autumn to reduce survivors. Note that some moths may survive by re-entering from broken windows or by emerging after treatment; hence repeated treatments and sealing openings improve efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of oils by flammability with compound spirit of nitre
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorize oils into three classes according to their reaction when compound spirit of nitre is poured on them: (1) make fire with great noise and explosion (marked **), (2) make a great noise with explosion but do not take fire (marked *), (3) make neither effervescence nor explosion (no mark). Further distinctions: vegetable (seed-derived/ethereal vs trunk/root-derived/ponderous), animal, and mineral oils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use origin (seed/trunk/root/animal/mineral), method of preparation (distillation vs expression), specific gravity (lighter or heavier than water), and volatility as predictors: essential oils from seeds tend to produce ebullition/explosion (often without flame), ponderous oils from trunks/roots and animal oils are likelier to take fire and flame. Expression-made vegetable oils (linseed, olive, almond) generally do not produce explosion or flame. Record the oil's source and distillation method when reporting flammability tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safe mixing procedure for oil and compound spirit of nitre
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred experimental procedure: use a gallipot spacious enough (4–5 ounces capacity for ~1 dram quantities), place oil in the vessel first, then pour the compound spirit of nitre onto the oil all at once (not gradually). Perform the experiment under a chimney or convenient draft, keep head at a safe distance, and scale vessel size with quantities used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warnings: perform under ventilation to remove offensive steams, never hold head close (sudden explosions may throw matter into the face), compound spirit loses virtue if stored long so prepare or use fresh, and enlarge vessel proportionally for larger amounts. These are explicit safety and procedural rules to reduce hazard and obtain reliable results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation of compound spirit of nitre (and common spirit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound spirit of nitre: distil equal parts saltpetre and oil of vitriol in a retort within a very hot sand furnace until deep red fumes settle in the receiver as a liquor, to be carefully preserved from air. Common spirit of nitre: mix 5–6 times clay to nitre and distil, optionally dephlegming and rectifying for strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a very strong fire during distillation (sand red-hot for hours). The compound spirit described combines igneous particles of spirit of nitre and those from oil of vitriol; the former is highly volatile and requires careful handling and preservation from air. Note that common spirit of nitre made with clay has different (weaker/uncertain) effects; the compound spirit is the reliable active reagent for the experiments described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive criterion: role of oil physical/chemical properties in accension
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider oil volatility, specific gravity, presence of volatile salts, and degree/type of distillation as determinants of whether an oil will produce ebullition, explosion, or flame with the compound spirit: light/ethereal seed oils are volatile and often explode without flame; ponderous oils (from trunks/roots) and animal oils are heavier and more apt to flame; mineral oils and expression-made oils often do little.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To influence outcome, one may add a more 'grumous' body (e.g., balsam of sulphur with oil of turpentine) to volatile oils to produce flame by slowing dissipation and allowing the fiery spirit time to penetrate. Interpret flammability as arising from both the oil's potential heat and inherent volatile salts which conspire with the compound spirit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of distillation conditions on oil flammability
rubrics_metrics.description: Oils subjected to longer and hotter distillation (ponderous oils) incorporate more 'igneous particles' and are more likely to take fire and sustain flame than oils distilled lightly or produced by expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or preparing oils for flammability tests, record distillation intensity and duration; expect ponderous oils to sink in water and to be more combustible, while light essential oils float and may be too volatile to sustain flame despite producing violent ebullition/explosion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation and interpretation of reactions in vacuum vs open air
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixing certain oil + compound spirit combinations in a vacuum (receiver cleared of air) can produce flame and sufficient gas/pressure to blow the receiver, demonstrating production of gases and expansion even without external air, unlike gunpowder which fails in vacuo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report whether reactions occur in vacuo and compare to known substances like gunpowder. Use vacuum experiments to infer generation of gases and internal pressure from the reacting liquids. Note the extraordinary nature if a small quantity (e.g., a dram and a half) produces sufficient pressure to shatter a receiver and account for the observed expansion qualitatively.
